articles_used.title: Wetterchaos an Thanksgiving in USA befürchtet
articles_used.summary_raw: Extreme Springflut und Überschwemmungen in Kalifornien - Sturmwarnung und viel Regen an der Ostküste. Pünktlich zu Thanksgiving könnte das Wetter die Reise- und Feiertagspläne vieler US-Amerikaner durcheinander bringen.

Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 26.11.2026 • 05:41 Uhr
Extreme Springflut und Überschwemmungen in Kalifornien - Sturmwarnung und viel Regen an der Ostküste. Pünktlich zu Thanksgiving könnte das Wetter die Reise- und Feiertagspläne vieler US-Amerikaner durcheinander bringen.
Im US-Bundesstaat Kalifornien hat es heftige Überschwemmungen an den Küsten gegeben. In der Bucht von San Francisco trafen Mittwoch gewaltige Wellen auf Land, wie der Nationale Wetterdienst NWS mitteilte.
Örtlichen Medienberichten zufolge erreichten die Wellen am Ocean Beach, dem wichtigsten Strand von San Francisco, eine Höhe von bis zu 9,14 Metern. Bereits am Vortag verzeichnete die Westküsten-Metropole die höchsten Wasserstände für einen November seit mehr als 40 Jahren.
Die ungewöhnlich hohen Flutwasserstände verschärften die Lage zusätzlich. Im Küstenort Pacifica nahe San Francisco brach ein Teil eines wegen Baufälligkeit gesperrten Holzpiers in den Pazifik. Entlang der Küste wurden Anwohner und Schaulustige gewarnt, sicheren Abstand von Flutzonen zu halten. Bürgermeister Daniel Lurie bot der Bevölkerung Sandsäcke zum Schutz gegen Überflutung an und rief dazu auf, unnötige Reisen zu vermeiden.
Flutwellen trafen die Küste von San Francisco, Kalifornien, USA.
Vielerorts werden die Feiern für Thanksgiving am Donnerstag wohl anders verlaufen als geplant. Neben reihenweisen Flugstreichungen und Straßensperrungen gibt es schon jetzt Schäden an der Infrastruktur. An der Ostküste zieht ein Sturm heran.
Im Bundesstaat New Jersey wird mit großflächigen Stromausfällen gerechnet, die bis zum Wochenende andauern könnte. In New York wurde eine berühmte Thanksgiving-Parade wegen Sturmwarnungen verschoben, in Teilen des gleichnamigen Bundesstaats vorsorglich der Notstand ausgerufen. Auch die Bewohner der US-Hauptstadt Washington wurde in einer Warnmeldung aufgerufen, in bestimmten Bereichen der Flussufer-Promenade am Potomac vorsichtig zu sein.
Thanksgiving - das Erntedankfest - zählt in den USA zu den wichtigsten nationalen Feiertagen im Jahr. Millionen sind unterwegs zu ihren Familien. Es gibt massiven Reiseverkehr, am ehesten vergleichbar mit den Zuständen in Deutschland rund um die Weihnachtsfeiertage.

articles_used.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles_used.summary_raw: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Unionand 12 other jurisdictions,including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announcedLiberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
Jamieson Greer, US trade representative
He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".
They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.
Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year
These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.
Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.
The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.
Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.
However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.
Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.
Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.
Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.
The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.
"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.
The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.
South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.
Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports
US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.
The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.

articles_used.title: EU-Haushalt: Kampf um bis zu zwei Billionen Euro
articles_used.summary_raw: Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 EU-Länder beraten bei einem Sondergipfel in Brüssel über den langfristigen EU-Haushalt. Dabei geht es auch um mögliche neue Einnahmequellen wie etwa eine Digitalsteuer.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 26.11.2026 • 05:00 Uhr
Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 EU-Länder beraten bei einem Sondergipfel in Brüssel über den langfristigen EU-Haushalt. Dabei geht es auch um mögliche neue Einnahmequellen wie etwa eine Digitalsteuer.
Es ist die ultimative Verhandlung. Der Kampf um bis zu zwei Billionen Euro geht in die entscheidenden Wochen. 2.000 Milliarden Euro. Mit wie viel Geld wollen die 27 Mitgliedstaaten die Europäische Union in den kommenden Jahren ausstatten?
Was als nüchterne Tabelle daherkommt, spiegelt wider, wer am Ende für sich am meisten erreicht hat. Es ist Macht in Zahlen. Die einen wollen die Höhe des EU-Haushaltes für die kommenden Jahre niedrig halten. Dazu gehört auch Deutschland. Andere argumentieren, nur mit mehr Geld ließen sich die großen Herausforderungen lösen. Zwei Tage lang werden die Staats- und Regierungschef der EU versuchen, dem großen Kompromiss ums große Geld näher zu kommen.
27.08.2026
Ratspräsident Costa muss den Konsens herstellen - und tourt dafür derzeit durch die Hauptstädte.mehr
"Es ist eigentlich die normale Choreografie dieser Verhandlung, dass es erst einen Gipfel gibt, der scheitern muss, damit der zweite dann gelingen kann", sagt Lucas Guttenberg von der Bertelsmann-Stiftung im Gespräch mit demARD-Studio Brüssel.
Der Direktor des Programms "Europas Zukunft" fragt sich aber auch, ob es dieses Drama unbedingt braucht. Im April stehen in Frankreich Präsidentschaftswahlen an. Gibt es also einen spätesten Zeitpunkt, bis zu dem die Verhandlungen um den EU-Haushalt abgeschlossen sein müssen? Darüber gehen in Brüssel die Einschätzungen auseinander.
Die Bertelsmann-Stiftung hat den"EU Budget Navigator"entwickelt. Es ist ein Online-Tool, mit dem sich die bisherigen Vorschläge für den EU-Haushalt vergleichen lassen. Den Anfang hatte die EU-Kommission mit knapp zwei Billionen Euro gemacht, am Wochenende legte Ratspräsident António Costa seine Version (rund 1,78 Billionen) vor.
15.10.2026
Die EU soll nicht so viel Geld ausgeben, findet Bundeskanzler Merz - und einige EU-Länder sehen das genauso.mehr
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz sieht darin einen ersten Schritt, das Gesamtvolumen sei aber weiterhin zu hoch. Wer will, kann im "Budget Navigator" auch einen Haushalt nach eigenen Vorstellungen basteln, kann selbst die Verteilung festlegen.
Traditionell sind die Regionalförderung und die Landwirtschaft die dominierenden Posten. Der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron macht kurz vor dem Gipfel klar: Gegenüber dem bisherigen Agrarbudget dürfe "kein einziger Euro" fehlen. Punkt.
Lucas Guttenberg von der Bertelsmann-Stiftung sagt: "In diesen Verhandlungen geht der Blick auf die gemeinsame Handlungsfähigkeit immer verloren. Stattdessen zählt: Wieviel bekomme ich eigentlich raus?" Es sind komplexe Verhandlungen. Vieles ist miteinander verflochten. So hat Merz zuletzt die weitere Finanzierung der Ukraine mit dem mehrjährigen Haushalt verknüpft.
15.10.2026
Auf dem heutigen EU-Gipfel geht es um bis zu zwei Billionen Euro. Kanzler Merz dringt auf Kürzungen.mehr
Auch mögliche neue Einnahmequellen gehören zur großen Gesamtrechnung. Ratspräsident Costa hat eine EU-Digitalsteuer vorgeschlagen. Bereits 2018 gab es einen entsprechenden Plan der EU-Kommission, der jedoch nie final beschlossen wurde. Es war von gut fünf Milliarden Euro jährlich die Rede.
Costa spricht davon, dass die Steuer "drei Prozent des jährlichen Nettoumsatzes aus Onlinewerbung, digitalen Vermittlungsdiensten und nutzergenerierten Daten" betragen soll. Sie würde für Unternehmen mit einem Umsatz von mindestens 50 Millionen Euro in der EU und mehr als 750 Millionen Euro weltweit gelten. Einige Mitgliedstaaten signalisierten Zustimmung. Irland jedoch, wo viele große Tech-Unternehmen ihren Europasitz haben, hat seine ablehnende Haltung bereits erklärt.
21.11.2026
Die EU-Staaten ringen um einen neuen Budgetplan. Gelingt eine Einigung bis Jahresende?mehr
Am Ende gilt: Dem finalen Kompromiss über das gesamte Haushaltspaket müssen alle EU-Staaten zustimmen. Der Europaabgeordnete Andreas Schwab, der für die CDU im Binnenmarkt-Ausschuss sitzt, sieht bei einer EU-Digitalsteuer durchaus kritische Punkte. Er sagt aber auch: "Dann wären wenigstens in allen EU-Staaten gleiche Bedingungen. Irland könnte da nicht ausscheren."
Auf jeden Fall müsste die EU wohl mit Ärger mit US-Präsident Donald Trump rechnen, der auf Instrumente gegen US-Tech-Konzerne chronisch gereizt reagiert. Wie viel Stress wird die EU für diese Einnahmen in Kauf nehmen?
Es gibt Mitgliedstaaten wie etwa Frankreich, Spanien und Italien, die bereits nationale Digitalsteuern eingeführt haben. Hier zeigt sich ein weiteres Detailproblem der Verhandlungen. Die EU kann zusätzliche Quellen für die Eigenmittel beschließen. Ratspräsident Costa schlägt hier unter anderem auch den Emissionshandel vor. Doch wenn das Geld aktuell schon in nationale Haushalte fließt, wäre es unter dem Strich keine wirkliche Entlastung.
Es ist die ultimative Verhandlung: Nettozahler gegen Nettoempfänger, größerer oder kleinerer Haushalt, Landwirtschaft oder Verteidigung? Wie viel Fortschritt ist von diesem Sondergipfel zu erwarten? Es ist Aufgabe von Ratspräsident Costa, den Weg zum finalen Kompromiss zu finden.
Den heutigen Tag werden die Staats- und Regierungschefs in der großen Runde beginnen, dann geht es in immer neue Konstellationen weiter. Auf der Basis dieser Gespräche dürfte Costa dann entscheiden, wie die Verhandlungen weiter ablaufen.
Bereits im Dezember steht der nächste Gipfel an. Manche Diplomaten sprechen bereits von einer möglichen Verlängerung im neuen Jahr. Für den Ratspräsidenten sind die Billionen-Verhandlungen auf jeden Fall eine persönliche Bewährungsprobe.

articles_used.title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
articles_used.summary_raw: The was the first time ever that the iconic celebration was delayed because of storms. New York expects damaging winds and heavy rainfall over the Thanksgiving holiday.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade
Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.
Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.
The last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.
A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.
The balloons will be deflated again and then re-inflated for Saturday
On Wednesday night, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for Long Island, New York City and Westchester County
The potent nor'easter is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.
Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.
"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.
Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.
Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.
"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."
Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".
Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.
This video can not be played
BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.
During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.
The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade was due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern US as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow,BBC Weatherreports.
The governor of the neighbouring state of New Jersey on Wednesday declared a state of emergency across the state's 21 counties, beginning at 18:00 local time (23:00 GMT).
Governor Mikie Sherrill's office said the powerful coastal storm is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall, and severe tidal flooding through Friday, with coastal and bayside communities facing the greatest risk. Sherrill urged residents to stay off the roads as much as possible once the storm arrives.
Originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade, the celebration, which also features live performers, debuted in 1924 as a way to boost holiday sales. It was founded by Macy's employees and their families.
From 1942 to 1944 New York went without the parade as the US directed materials like rubber and helium toward the country's war effort.
The 2.5mi (4km) procession route begins at Macy's Herald Square flagship store and concludes in Manhattan's Upper West Side, with performers and spectators lining the streets to greet Santa Claus and ring in the holiday season.
Country artist Megan Moroney and Grammy nominee Teddy Swims were slated to perform at the flagship store, but it is unclear whether they, along with the dozens of celebrities and float performers on the roster, would be returning on Saturday.

articles_used.title: SpaceX darf eine Million Satelliten für KI-Rechenzentren ins All schicken
articles_used.summary_raw: SpaceX plant im All ein Netz aus Satelliten, die als Rechenzentren dienen sollen. Die US-Behörden haben das Vorhaben nun erlaubt. Ziel ist es, die enorme Nachfrage nach Rechenleistung für Künstliche Intelligenz zu befriedigen.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 26.11.2026 • 02:58 Uhr
SpaceX plant im All ein Netz aus Satelliten, die als Rechenzentren dienen sollen. Die US-Behörden haben das Vorhaben nun erlaubt. Ziel ist es, die enorme Nachfrage nach Rechenleistung für Künstliche Intelligenz zu befriedigen.
Das Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX des Milliardärs Elon Musk darf bis zu eine Million Satelliten zur Errichtung von Weltraum-Rechenzentren für KI-Anwendungen in den Erdorbit schicken. Zum Vergleich: Derzeit kreisen dort etwa 17.000 Satelliten, mehr als die Hälfte davon von SpaceX.
Die US-Regulierungsbehörde FCC erteilte dem Projekt des Konzerns mit dem Namen "Starmind" eine Genehmigung. "Indem sie Rechenkapazitäten über die Erdoberfläche hinaus verlagern, werden SpaceX und die zahlreichen Wettbewerber, die an ihren eigenen Datenzentren im Orbit arbeiten, den Anforderungen der Zeit gerecht", sagte FCC-Chef Brendan Carr. Die Genehmigung ebnet nun den Weg für ein Konzept, das im Mittelpunkt von Musks Präsentation im Rahmen des Börsengangs von SpaceX gestanden hatte.
Die Satelliten sollen in einer niedrigen Erdumlaufbahn in geringem Abstand zueinander positioniert werden, um eine zuverlässige Datenübertragung untereinander zu ermöglichen. Sie sollen über die bereits im All befindlichen Satelliten des SpaceX-Internetdienstes Starlink Daten zur Erde übertragen. Der US-Chiphersteller Nvidia soll eigens für den Einsatz im Weltraum konzipierte Prozessoren der neuesten Generation liefern.
15.11.2026
Erstmals landete die etwa 50 Meter große obere Raketenstufe wieder auf der Erde.mehr
Allerdings gibt es für die Errichtung von weltraumgestützten Rechenzentren auch technische Hürden. Sie brauchen sehr große Solarmodule zur Stromerzeugung sowie ausgefeilte Kühltechnologien und auch Systeme zur Übertragung riesiger Datenmengen zur Erde. So müssen die Prozessoren der hohen Strahlenbelastung im All standhalten. Weitere Herausforderungen sind extreme Temperaturen und mögliche Schäden durch Weltraumschrott und Mikrometeoriten.
Ausgeklappt soll die Photovoltaikanlage SpaceX zufolge jeweils eine Flügelspannweite von 75 Metern haben. Im rechten Winkel dazu entfalten sich dann Radiatoren mit Kühlflüssigkeit. Auch sie sehen wie Flügel aus, sind etwa 30 Meter lang und haben eine Fläche von 160 Quadratmetern. Die Energie soll die Sonne liefern, die Kühlung erledigt sich laut den Ingenieuren praktisch von selbst, weil es im Weltraum so kalt ist.
03.02.2026
Es ist eine Fusion der Superlative. Die KI-Sparte kann dadurch leicht mit Kapital versorgt werden.mehr
Ein Vorteil von Rechenzentren im All ist die Möglichkeit, Sonnenenergie kontinuierlich zu nutzen. In einer geeigneten sonnensynchronen Umlaufbahn können Solarzellen nach Berechnungen von Google bis zu achtmal so viel Energie liefern wie auf der Erde.
Musk hatte im Februar für den Aufbau von Rechenzentren im All seine KI-Firma xAI und SpaceX zusammengelegt. Der wachsende Energiebedarf für Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) könne auf der Erde nicht ohne Belastungen für Menschen und Umwelt gedeckt werden, argumentierte Musk damals.
Gemäß der Lizenz muss SpaceX spätestens im November 2033 mit dem Einsatz beginnen. Nach Angaben der FCC muss SpaceX darüber hinaus zehn Prozent der maximal genehmigten Satelliten bis November 2035 ins All bringen, bis November 2038 müssen es dann 50 Prozent sein.
Mit Informationen von Carsten Kühntopp, ARD-Studio Washington.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.
Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights are expected to resume by around 22:00 local time, the FAA told the BBC.
The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.
The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.
Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.
Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travelers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.
The Miami-Dade area is under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.
A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

articles_used.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
articles_used.summary_raw: Somalia relies heavily on foreign funding and military support for its very survival.
articles_used.full_text:
Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support
Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.
The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.
Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.
The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.
The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.
Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.
Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.
The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.
With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.
The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.
Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.
He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.
"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.
The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.
Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.
Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia?
Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.
In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.
His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.
Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.
They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.
Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.
But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.
He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.
Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.
He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.
He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.
"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.
During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.
Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007
Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.
He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.
It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.
But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.
Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are  under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.
This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.
The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.
The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.
Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.
Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.
Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.
But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.
The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.
Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government
This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.
A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.
The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain.
Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.
Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.
"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said.
He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.
Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?
Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.
Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.
Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid.
Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.
But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.
He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.
That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.
Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support
Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.
The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.
The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.
The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support.
For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.
He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.
But Guleid remains far less optimistic.
He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.
For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.
Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

articles_used.title: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
articles_used.summary_raw: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms and flooding, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak inthe state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.
Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.
In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.
While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by thestrongest El Niño weather pattern on record.
Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.
The US department store chainMacy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Paradein New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

articles_used.title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
articles_used.summary_raw: The movement to repeal women's right to vote has gained traction amongst some very conservative Christians.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
Watch: Doug Wilson talks about DC outpost of church where Hegseth, other members of Trump administration worship
"Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.
Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.
A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.
In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.
The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.
Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles.
"In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC.
"I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."
Have the American Pope and the American administration fallen out?
Pete Hegseth brings combative style as face of Trump's war in Iran
But while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.
The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.
His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".
Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.
Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."
Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.
Pete Hegseth has thanked Pastor Doug Wilson for his "mentorship"
Of all his views, it is his statements on women's suffrage that have garnered the most headlines.
Wilson favours "household voting", where the head of the home – usually a man – votes on behalf of their family.  It's the system used for elections within his church, although the women in Wilson's family do vote in civic elections in order to counter votes of liberals, he says.
He says only in "odd" circumstances,  such as divorce or bereavement or "where the husband was a quadriplegic," should women assume the role of head of household. Just 7% of votes in Wilson's church polity are cast by women.
When challenged by the BBC, he admitted it was a system that gave men "outsized influence".
Wilson says that repealing the 19th Amendment is "low" on the list of priorities for him and his congregation. But, he adds, "we do think it".
Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, says Wilson's beliefs are misogynistic and extreme - part of a world view that says women should be in complete submission to men in every part of their lives.
It is extremely unlikely that the 19th Amendment would be repealed - it would require either a proposal from two-thirds of the House and Senate or two-thirds of the state legislatures. Three quarters of states would then need to ratify it.
Still, says Ingersoll, the threat to women's rights should be taken seriously.
"It's not unlike the battle that they waged against Roe versus Wade," she says, referencing the Supreme Court decision that granted women the right to an abortion. It was overturned in 2022, after years of legal battles that restricted women's access to abortion.
"Thirty years ago, people would have said, oh, they're not gonna undo abortion rights.
"But they chipped away and they kept chipping away until they were able to overturn it. And I see this as directly parallel."
While Wilson says overturning the 19th Amendment could take a century or more, there are conservative Christians who are pushing for women to have their right to vote removed more immediately.
Last February, pastor Dale Partridge posted on Instagram saying "We will repeal the 19th Amendment within ten years".
Partridge, who has around 900k followers across social media, credits Wilson as being someone who "broke the ice" for "strong politics and theology".
Partridge has said that "the majority of women are not capable of responsible voting" because too many of them are liberal.
He also frequently collaborates on podcasts with another conservative pastor named Joel Webbon.
Webbon, whose New Christian Right YouTube channel  has more than 190k subscribers, has said that women's "desires are wicked". The solution, he claims, is to "take away women's vote". He was once friendly with Wilson, although they have since fallen out.
"Those guys have overshot by a long way," says Wilson of the two younger pastors. "They are disruptors and basically rage baiting."
So what might be driving those who support the effort?
Kelly Marino, an associate professor at Sacred Heart University who studies women's suffrage, says that the last decade has seen big wins for the women's rights movement, and "liberal political ideology" in general.
But, she argues, "any time where there was sort of this peak of feminism, there've been people who respond aggressively and try to push back".
Added to that are the high levels of uncertainty and conflict that have characterised the post-Covid period.
"I think there's been this craving for tradition and things that felt safe," Marino says.
That, she says, can be seen in the popularity of notions such as being a "tradwife" or "soft girl", who reject career goals in favour of traditionally female roles of wife and mother.
Marino says that while she doesn't think the constitution could be changed in the immediate future, the conversation around repealing the 19th Amendment is shaping the way people think about women's roles in general.
Canon Corsello, the Vicar at Washington Cathedral, sees the midterm election results as a repudiation of the push against women's rights.
"Cultural issues did not translate in this election", she says. "When people are preaching love, empathy, inclusion... that actually resonated with people".
Wilson's views have, however, been gaining ground beyond the US. The CREC has more than 30 churches internationally, including in Poland, Japan and Brazil.
The latter country has seen its own movement of right-wing influencers pressing for the removal of women's suffrage, with some leaning on religious language to make their point.
Wilson wants to continue expanding his brand of Christianity around the world, and has recently accepted a church in England into his network.
While CREC churches in each country have their own distinct characteristics, Wilson says their core beliefs are the same.
When it comes to the US, he says his ideal scenario would be for his congregations to "to practice what we believe in the church and for outsiders to look at that and envy it and say, man, that seems like a good system".

articles_used.title: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
articles_used.summary_raw: After eight years of Socialist-led rule, snap elections are taking place on Sunday with conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo vying to win office.
articles_used.full_text:
The People's Party of Alberto Núñez Feijóo is narrowly ahead in most opinion polls
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.
He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on Feijóo andwho else to watch in this election - read here.
Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.
Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration.
Spain saw its first general strike for 14 years this month over a shortage of housing and high rental costs
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.
The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.
Pedro Sánchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez has played an important role in the election campaign
Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about Feijóo's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality – and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.
Their big themes are "national priority" – putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Pedro Sánchez (left), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (centre) and Santiago Abascal (right)
Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto Nuñez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
Feijóo's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
Feijóo has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain had ever seen, and a number of cases have involved Sánchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento más trascendental.
His former transport minister José Luis Ábalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David Sánchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
Feijóo has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."
Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.
"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
The leader of Vox, Santiago Abascal, is hoping to double his party's seats in parliament
Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time Feijóo had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y León.
The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, Aragón, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia.
Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.
Sánchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.
To win a seat, a party has to win 3% of the vote in a province, but in smaller provinces with fewer seats parties generally need more than that.

articles_used.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
articles_used.summary_raw: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
articles_used.full_text:
Protests on the streets of France over students' concerns and the cost of living have  been marked by looting and unrest in recent weeks
France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027,  unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.
With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.
In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.
That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.
But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.
"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."
On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.
His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.
The protests started as an expression of anger at conditions in high schools
In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).
Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.
So with the soft-left emasculated,  the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right.  But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.
"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper.  "But it is looking increasingly probable."
In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote.  Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.
Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling.  They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal;  the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau;  and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.
David Lisnard (centre) has seen membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie jump to more than 100,000
Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.
But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.
According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists.  Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.
"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns.  In the middle… nothing."
Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.
"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions.  We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.
"What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary.  It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."
For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'.  Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."
Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.
According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration.
"But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."
Emmanuel Macron is now considered a politically toxic figure in France
With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.
Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb.  The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."
In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.
Possible, but hardly a good bet.
For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."
Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained.  Polarisation is their friend,  so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.
The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.

articles_used.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
articles_used.summary_raw: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.
Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.
On Wednesday evening, the Army said that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.
President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".
"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.
Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.
"Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete," the Army added.
Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin also said on social media that in the hours after the detonation "all EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead".
The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.
He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site.
"We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.
Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down.
The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened.
"We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened.
"The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."
Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday.
"I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.
Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said on X that his state was "seeing little to no impact" from the blast. In a press release, he said he was directing state agencies to remain on standby for any "unanticipated impact".
The Iowa site is only 10 miles (16 km) from the Illinois border.
But there is also caution from some.
Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".
Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".
Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.
In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.
It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.
The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds.
But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.
Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

script.intro: Guten Morgen und herzlich willkommen zu unserem Nachrichten-Digest! Es ist Thanksgiving-Zeit in den USA, aber das Wetter sorgt für Chaos. Auch in Europa tut sich einiges und wir schauen auf die neuesten Entwicklungen.

segments.headline: Wetterchaos zu Thanksgiving in den USA erwartet: Von Springflut bis Sturmwarnung
segments.narration: In den USA herrscht pünktlich zum Thanksgiving-Fest extremes Wetter. Kalifornien erlebt heftige Überschwemmungen an den Küsten, mit Wellen von bis zu 9 Metern Höhe in der Bucht von San Francisco. Dort brach sogar ein Teil eines Piers zusammen. Auch an der Ostküste zieht ein Sturm heran, der in New Jersey großflächige Stromausfälle verursachen könnte. Die traditionelle Thanksgiving-Parade in New York wurde wegen der Sturmwarnungen auf Samstag verschoben. Diese Wetterlage könnte die Reisepläne von Millionen Amerikanern erheblich beeinträchtigen.
segments.summary_short: Extreme Wetterbedingungen in den USA, darunter Springfluten in Kalifornien und ein Sturm an der Ostküste, stören landesweit die Thanksgiving-Reise- und Feiertagspläne, was zur Verschiebung der New Yorker Parade führt.

segments.headline: FedEx-Flugzeug überschießt Landebahn in Miami – Flugverkehr kurzzeitig unterbrochen
segments.narration: Inmitten des Reisechaos zu Thanksgiving gab es auch am Miami International Airport einen Zwischenfall: Ein FedEx-Flugzeug ist gestern Abend über die Landebahn hinausgeschossen. Die Federal Aviation Administration musste daraufhin Flüge nach Miami vorübergehend einstellen und die meisten Start- und Landebahnen schließen. Glücklicherweise gab es keine Verletzten, und der Flugverkehr sollte gegen 22:00 Uhr Ortszeit wieder aufgenommen werden. Der Vorfall ereignete sich an einem der verkehrsreichsten Reisetage des Jahres.
segments.summary_short: Ein FedEx-Flugzeug überschoss die Landebahn am Miami International Airport, was zu einer kurzzeitigen Einstellung des Flugverkehrs und Sperrungen führte, aber glücklicherweise gab es keine Verletzten.

segments.headline: USA kündigen neue Zölle gegen China, EU und weitere Länder an
segments.narration: Bleiben wir in den USA, aber wechseln wir das Thema zur Wirtschaft: Präsident Donald Trump treibt seine Handelspolitik weiter voran und hat neue Zölle gegen eine Reihe von Ländern angekündigt, darunter China und die Europäische Union. China sieht sich mit den höchsten Zollsätzen von bis zu 40 Prozent konfrontiert. Diese Maßnahmen sollen im nächsten Jahr in Kraft treten, nach öffentlichen Anhörungen. Kritiker warnen jedoch, dass Zölle die Inflation anheizen und die Preise für Verbraucher in die Höhe treiben könnten.
segments.summary_short: Die USA haben neue Zölle gegen wichtige Handelspartner wie China und die EU angekündigt, um Trumps Handelspolitik voranzutreiben, was jedoch Bedenken hinsichtlich Inflation und globaler Handelsdämpfung aufwirft.

segments.headline: EU-Haushalt: Kampf um bis zu zwei Billionen Euro und eine Digitalsteuer
segments.narration: Von den USA geht es direkt nach Europa, wo die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 EU-Länder über den langfristigen EU-Haushalt verhandeln. Es geht um nicht weniger als zwei Billionen Euro. Deutschland plädiert für einen niedrigeren Haushalt, während andere Länder mehr Geld für die Bewältigung großer Herausforderungen fordern. Auch neue Einnahmequellen wie eine EU-Digitalsteuer stehen zur Debatte. Diese würde große Tech-Unternehmen betreffen und könnte etwa drei Prozent des jährlichen Nettoumsatzes aus Online-Werbung einbringen. Ein kompliziertes Geflecht von Interessen, denn alle 27 Mitgliedstaaten müssen dem finalen Kompromiss zustimmen. Ratspräsident Costa muss hier den Konsens herstellen.
segments.summary_short: Die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs verhandeln über den langfristigen EU-Haushalt von bis zu zwei Billionen Euro, wobei Deutschland für Kürzungen plädiert und eine EU-Digitalsteuer als mögliche neue Einnahmequelle diskutiert wird.

segments.headline: Spanien vor vorgezogenen Wahlen: Richtungsentscheidung für das Land
segments.narration: Gleich um die Ecke in Spanien stehen am Sonntag vorgezogene Parlamentswahlen an. Nach acht Jahren unter sozialistischer Führung steht das Land an einem Scheideweg. Die konservative Volkspartei von Alberto Núñez Feijóo liegt in den meisten Umfragen knapp vor den Sozialisten, wird aber voraussichtlich die Unterstützung der rechtsextremen Vox-Partei benötigen. Themen wie die hohen Lebenshaltungskosten, Korruption und Immigration dominieren den Wahlkampf.
segments.summary_short: Spanien steht vor vorgezogenen Parlamentswahlen am Sonntag, bei denen die konservative Volkspartei knapp führt und wahrscheinlich die Unterstützung der rechtsextremen Vox-Partei braucht, während Themen wie Lebenshaltungskosten, Korruption und Immigration den Wahlkampf prägen.

segments.headline: Frankreichs politische Mitte in der Krise vor der Präsidentschaftswahl
segments.narration: Ein Blick nach Frankreich zeigt, dass die politische Mitte dort vor der Präsidentschaftswahl im April 2027 vor einem Debakel steht. Umfragen deuten darauf hin, dass Marine Le Pen von der extremen Rechten und Jean-Luc Mélenchon von der extremen Linken dominieren könnten. Persönliche Rivalitäten und eine fehlende gemeinsame Vision verhindern bisher eine starke Herausforderung aus der Mitte. Die sogenannten 'Alleinverwalter der Vernunft' haben ihre Vernunft verloren, so ein politischer Beobachter.
segments.summary_short: Die politische Mitte Frankreichs steht vor der Präsidentschaftswahl 2027 vor einem potenziellen Debakel, da Marine Le Pen und Jean-Luc Mélenchon in Umfragen dominieren und es der Mitte an geeinten Kandidaten fehlt.

segments.headline: US-Pastor fordert Aufhebung des Frauenwahlrechts – wachsender Einfluss konservativer Ansichten
segments.narration: Eine Meldung aus den USA sorgt für Aufsehen: Der konservative Pastor Doug Wilson, ein Mentor von US-Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth, fordert die Aufhebung des 19. Zusatzartikels zur Verfassung, der Frauen das Wahlrecht gewährt. Wilson vertritt die Ansicht, dass eine von Männern geführte Gesellschaft ein 'großer Segen' sei und möchte ein 'Haushaltswahlrecht' einführen, bei dem der Haushaltsvorstand – meist der Mann – für die Familie abstimmt. Obwohl seine Ansichten extrem sind, gewinnen sie laut Beobachtern an Unterstützung, auch durch Verbindungen zu einflussreichen Persönlichkeiten. Allerdings wird die Umsetzung als unwahrscheinlich angesehen.
segments.summary_short: Der konservative US-Pastor Doug Wilson fordert die Aufhebung des Frauenwahlrechts und ein 'Haushaltswahlrecht', was trotz seiner extremen Ansichten an Einfluss gewinnt, aber als verfassungsrechtlich unwahrscheinlich gilt.

segments.headline: Somalia vor neuer Instabilität? Abzug ausländischer Truppen und politische Streitigkeiten
segments.narration: Zum Abschluss werfen wir einen Blick nach Somalia: Das Land steht vor einer neuen Bewährungsprobe, da ausländische Truppen abziehen und politische Streitigkeiten die geplanten direkten Wahlen gefährden. Analysten befürchten, dass diese Situation die islamistische Miliz al-Shabab ermutigen und sogar zur Übernahme der Hauptstadt Mogadischu führen könnte, ähnlich dem Fall Afghanistans durch die Taliban. Trotz der Beteiligung der Afrikanischen Union kontrolliert al-Shabab bereits große Teile des Landes. Die somalischen Sicherheitskräfte könnten ohne externe Unterstützung Schwierigkeiten haben, die Sicherheit zu gewährleisten. Dies führt zu großer Unsicherheit in der Region.
segments.summary_short: Somalia steht aufgrund des Abzugs ausländischer Truppen und interner politischer Konflikte vor einer erhöhten Instabilität, was die Gefahr einer Machtübernahme durch al-Shabab erhöht und die nationalen Sicherheitskräfte überfordert.

segments.headline: SpaceX erhält Genehmigung für eine Million KI-Satelliten im All
segments.narration: Eine spannende Entwicklung aus der Welt der Technologie: Elon Musks Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX hat die Genehmigung erhalten, bis zu eine Million Satelliten in den Erdorbit zu schicken, die als Rechenzentren für Künstliche Intelligenz dienen sollen. Das Projekt namens 'Starmind' soll die enorme Nachfrage nach Rechenleistung befriedigen und die Kapazitäten über die Erde hinaus verlagern. Die Satelliten, ausgestattet mit speziellen Nvidia-Prozessoren, müssen jedoch technische Hürden wie hohe Strahlenbelastung und extreme Temperaturen überwinden. Der Beginn des Einsatzes ist für November 2033 geplant.

segments.headline: Kontrollierte Explosion von Giftstoffen in Iowa von US-Armee als 'riesiger Erfolg' gefeiert
segments.narration: Und noch eine kurze Meldung aus den USA: Die US-Armee hat die Sprengung von fast fünf Tonnen giftiger Sprengstoffe in Iowa als 'riesigen Erfolg' gefeiert. Diese Operation hatte im Vorfeld Ängste vor Gesundheits- und Umweltproblemen ausgelöst und wurde mehrfach verschoben. Nach der Explosion wurden keine Bleiwerte in der Luft gemessen, und erste Bodenproben waren vielversprechend. Lokale Bewohner äußerten sich erleichtert, da sie weder etwas spürten noch sahen. Auch Präsident Trump lobte die Maßnahmen, die 'alle Erwartungen übertroffen' hätten.

script.full_text: Guten Morgen und herzlich willkommen zu unserem Nachrichten-Digest! Es ist Thanksgiving-Zeit in den USA, aber das Wetter sorgt für Chaos. Auch in Europa tut sich einiges und wir schauen auf die neuesten Entwicklungen.In den USA herrscht pünktlich zum Thanksgiving-Fest extremes Wetter. Kalifornien erlebt heftige Überschwemmungen an den Küsten, mit Wellen von bis zu 9 Metern Höhe in der Bucht von San Francisco. Dort brach sogar ein Teil eines Piers zusammen. Auch an der Ostküste zieht ein Sturm heran, der in New Jersey großflächige Stromausfälle verursachen könnte. Die traditionelle Thanksgiving-Parade in New York wurde wegen der Sturmwarnungen auf Samstag verschoben. Diese Wetterlage könnte die Reisepläne von Millionen Amerikanern erheblich beeinträchtigen.Inmitten des Reisechaos zu Thanksgiving gab es auch am Miami International Airport einen Zwischenfall: Ein FedEx-Flugzeug ist gestern Abend über die Landebahn hinausgeschossen. Die Federal Aviation Administration musste daraufhin Flüge nach Miami vorübergehend einstellen und die meisten Start- und Landebahnen schließen. Glücklicherweise gab es keine Verletzten, und der Flugverkehr sollte gegen 22:00 Uhr Ortszeit wieder aufgenommen werden. Der Vorfall ereignete sich an einem der verkehrsreichsten Reisetage des Jahres.Bleiben wir in den USA, aber wechseln wir das Thema zur Wirtschaft: Präsident Donald Trump treibt seine Handelspolitik weiter voran und hat neue Zölle gegen eine Reihe von Ländern angekündigt, darunter China und die Europäische Union.
